laws.title: Moroccan Mint Tea — Refusing is Deeply Rude
laws.subtitle: Three glasses of mint tea; bargaining expected
laws.fullDescription: Moroccan mint tea (atay) is a ritual — it's poured three times from height (for froth) and the three glasses symbolise life, love, and death. Never refuse offered tea. Bargaining (haggling) is expected in souks — accepting the first price is considered naive. Dress modestly outside of beach resorts. Remove shoes before entering homes and mosques.
laws.penalty: No legal penalty — refusing tea or hospitality causes genuine offence in Moroccan culture.
exceptions: Medinas (old cities) are more traditional than modern districts
Agadir beach resort area has more relaxed dress codes

quiz.q: In Moroccan tea culture, how many glasses of mint tea are typically served?
quiz.explanation: Three glasses of Moroccan mint tea are traditionally served — symbolising life, love, and death.

laws.title: LGBTQ+ Laws — Criminal in Morocco
laws.subtitle: Penal Code Art. 489 — Up to 3 years imprisonment
laws.fullDescription: Same-sex relations are illegal in Morocco under Article 489 of the Penal Code, carrying up to 3 years imprisonment and a fine. Public displays of same-sex affection can lead to arrest. Morocco is not safe for LGBTQ+ travellers to be open. Raids on private gatherings have occurred. Some famous resort areas are more tolerant in practice but offer no legal protection.
laws.penalty: Same-sex relations: 6 months to 3 years imprisonment + MAD 120–1,200 fine.
exceptions: None in law — enforcement is selective but real
Major resort areas may be more tolerant in practice

quiz.q: What does Article 489 of Morocco's Penal Code criminalise?
quiz.explanation: Morocco's Article 489 criminalises same-sex relations with up to 3 years imprisonment — LGBTQ+ travellers face real legal risk.

laws.title: Dress Code — Medinas and Religious Sites
laws.subtitle: Public decency laws — Shoulders and knees covered required
laws.fullDescription: Morocco has no formal nationwide dress code law, but local ordinances and public decency norms mean that immodest dress (shorts above the knee, bare shoulders, revealing tops) in medinas, markets, and near mosques can attract unwanted attention or police intervention. Women face significantly more scrutiny. Non-Muslims cannot enter mosques (except a few exceptions). Respect for Ramadan fasting is legally required in many contexts.
laws.penalty: No fixed legal penalty for tourists — but public decency violations can result in police intervention. Eating in public during Ramadan daylight hours: possible fine.
exceptions: Resort areas like Agadir beach: relaxed dress
Riads and tourist accommodations: private space rules apply
laws.sourceLabel: Morocco Ministry of Tourism — Cultural Guidelines

quiz.q: Can non-Muslims enter mosques in Morocco?
options: No — most mosques are closed to non-Muslims
quiz.explanation: Most Moroccan mosques are closed to non-Muslims — a notable exception is the Hassan II Mosque in Casablanca which allows non-Muslim visitors on guided tours.

laws.title: Alcohol — Legal But Restricted; Ramadan Complications
laws.subtitle: Available in licensed venues; Ramadan sales restricted
laws.fullDescription: Alcohol is legal in Morocco for non-Muslims in licensed hotels, bars, and restaurants. However, it is not openly available in medinas, near mosques, or in traditional areas. During Ramadan, many restaurants and bars stop serving alcohol entirely (some close). Supermarkets with alcohol licences exist (Marjane, Carrefour) in modern urban areas. Drinking in public (streets, parks) is illegal and can attract police attention. Muslims selling alcohol to other Muslims is technically an offence.
laws.penalty: Public drinking: police intervention, fine, possible arrest. Disorderly conduct while drunk: imprisonment.
exceptions: Licensed tourist hotels always serve alcohol
Major modern supermarkets in tourist cities
Residents with non-Moroccan passports in licensed venues

quiz.q: Where is it safest to buy alcohol in Morocco as a tourist?
options: Licensed tourist hotels, bars, and specific modern supermarkets
quiz.explanation: Alcohol in Morocco is available in licensed tourist hotels, bars, and some modern supermarkets (e.g. Carrefour, Marjane) — but not in medinas, near mosques, or in traditional areas.

laws.title: Cannabis — Illegal But Widespread; Rif Mountain Production
laws.subtitle: Law 13-21 passed 2021 — Limited legalisation for medical/industrial use only
laws.fullDescription: Cannabis (kif) has been grown in Morocco's Rif Mountains for centuries — Morocco is historically one of the world's largest cannabis resin (hashish) producers. Despite cultural and economic presence, recreational cannabis remains illegal. In 2021, Law 13-21 legalised cannabis for medical, industrial, and cosmetic purposes under strict licensing. Possession for personal use is still criminalised. Tourists in Chefchaouen (a notorious blue city cannabis hub) are frequently approached by dealers — possession can lead to arrest even in seemingly relaxed areas.
laws.penalty: Cannabis possession: 1 month to 2 years imprisonment + MAD 1,200–5,000 fine. Trafficking: 10–30 years.
exceptions: Licensed medical/industrial production under Law 13-21 (since 2021)
No recreational exemption — still illegal to possess for personal use

quiz.q: Despite being a major cannabis producer, what is the status of recreational cannabis possession in Morocco?
options: Still fully illegal — prosecuted with imprisonment
Legal in the Rif Mountains only
quiz.explanation: Morocco's 2021 Law 13-21 only legalised cannabis for medical and industrial purposes — recreational possession remains fully illegal and prosecuted.

laws.title: Unmarried Couples Sharing Hotel Rooms — Technically Illegal, Inconsistently Enforced
laws.subtitle: Moroccan Penal Code Article 490 — 'Illicit sexual relations' between unmarried persons
laws.fullDescription: Article 490 of the Moroccan Penal Code criminalises sexual relations between unmarried persons ('relations sexuelles illicites'). In practice, this law creates a grey area for unmarried couples — whether tourists or locals — seeking to share a hotel room. Legally, hotels are permitted to ask for proof of marriage and refuse accommodation to unmarried mixed-sex couples. Enforcement is wildly inconsistent: international hotels in Marrakech, Casablanca, and Agadir generally ignore the rule entirely and cater to Western tourists without question. Smaller, locally-run riads and budget hotels in medinas are more likely to enforce it. Moroccan nationals face greater risk than foreigners — local unmarried couples have been prosecuted under this law. For foreign tourists, the practical risk is low in tourist-facing hotels, but higher if staying in traditional guesthouses or smaller towns. Same-sex couples face even greater risk: homosexuality is also criminalised under Article 489.
laws.penalty: Conviction under Article 490: up to 1 month imprisonment. Hotels that knowingly facilitate unmarried cohabitation can also face legal consequences.
exceptions: International and tourist-class hotels routinely and openly accommodate unmarried foreign couples without issue
Moroccan nationals married under foreign law are generally accepted with a marriage certificate

quiz.q: What does Moroccan Penal Code Article 490 technically criminalise that affects unmarried tourist couples?
options: Sharing a meal with someone of the opposite sex
Travelling together without a marriage certificate
Sexual relations between unmarried persons — including unmarried couples sharing hotel rooms
quiz.explanation: Article 490 of the Moroccan Penal Code criminalises sexual relations between unmarried persons, which technically extends to unmarried couples sharing a hotel room — though enforcement against foreign tourists at international hotels is very rare.

laws.title: Ramadan Public Eating — Article 222 Criminalises Eating in Daylight
laws.subtitle: Moroccan Penal Code Article 222 — 1–6 months imprisonment + fine for Muslims eating publicly in Ramadan
laws.fullDescription: Article 222 of the Moroccan Penal Code criminalises any Muslim who ‘publicly and ostentatiously breaks the fast’ during Ramadan without a valid reason, with penalties of 1 to 6 months imprisonment + fines of 200 to 500 dirhams. The provision is controversial but remains enforced. In practice most cafés and restaurants close during daylight; those that remain open (in tourist zones such as Marrakech’s Gueliz, Casablanca’s Maarif, and coastal resort hotels) serve only non-Muslim foreigners and are legally obliged to use curtains or screened interiors. Eating, drinking (including water), or smoking publicly on the street during daylight in Ramadan is taboo and can draw fines or arrest of Moroccan citizens; tourists are not typically prosecuted but are strongly advised to be discreet out of respect. Large hotels serve tourists all day. Public transport runs normally, though many businesses shift hours. Iftar (the breaking of the fast at sunset) is a communal event foreigners are frequently invited to join.
laws.penalty: Moroccan citizen breaking fast publicly during Ramadan: 1 to 6 months imprisonment + fine 200–500 dirhams under Article 222. Non-Muslim foreigners are not subject to Article 222 but can face fines under public-order by-laws for provocative public eating.
exceptions: Non-Muslim foreigners are exempt from Article 222 but expected to be discreet
Hotels, airport zones, and tourist-zone cafés may serve non-Muslims all day under screened conditions
laws.sourceLabel: Moroccan Penal Code Article 222 — Secretary-General of the Government

quiz.q: Under Moroccan law, which article criminalises a Muslim publicly breaking the Ramadan fast?
options: There is no such law — it is customary only
quiz.explanation: Article 222 of the Moroccan Penal Code criminalises a Muslim who publicly and ostentatiously breaks the Ramadan fast — 1 to 6 months imprisonment plus fines. Non-Muslim foreigners are exempt but expected to be discreet.

laws.title: Ramadan Observance — Non-Muslims Eating Publicly Can Cause Legal Issues
laws.subtitle: Moroccan Penal Code Art. 222 — Breaking fast publicly: up to 6 months imprisonment
laws.fullDescription: Morocco is a predominantly Muslim country and Ramadan is observed with deep seriousness. Article 222 of the Moroccan Penal Code makes it a criminal offence for Muslims to eat, drink, or smoke publicly during Ramadan fasting hours — punishable by up to 6 months imprisonment. While non-Muslims are not subject to this law, eating publicly in front of fasting Moroccans in traditional areas is considered highly disrespectful and can create confrontation. Many restaurants close during the day during Ramadan. After sunset (iftar), the whole country comes alive with festive eating and socialising. The medinas of Marrakech, Fes, and Chefchaouen have specific areas where tourist restaurants remain open discreetly during the day.
laws.penalty: Muslim breaking fast publicly (Art. 222): up to 6 months imprisonment. Non-Muslim eating publicly: no criminal penalty but possible confrontation.
exceptions: Non-Muslims are legally exempt from the public fasting rules
Cafés and restaurants designated for tourists may operate discreetly

quiz.q: Under Morocco's Penal Code Article 222, what is the maximum penalty for a Muslim breaking fast publicly during Ramadan?
quiz.explanation: Morocco's Penal Code Article 222 imposes up to 6 months imprisonment for Muslims who break the Ramadan fast publicly — eating, drinking, or smoking during fasting hours is a criminal offence for Muslim citizens.

laws.title: Moroccan Family Code (Moudawwana) — Marriage, Divorce, and Inheritance Laws
laws.subtitle: Morocco's 2004 family code reform expanded women's rights; further reform debated in 2023
laws.fullDescription: Morocco's Family Code (Moudawwana), reformed in 2004, significantly expanded women's legal rights. Women can now initiate divorce without proving fault (khul divorce), minimum marriage age raised to 18 (though courts can grant exceptions for minors with judicial approval). Polygamy requires court authorization and notification of existing wife. Custody of children defaults to mother until remarriage, then transfers to father. Inheritance law still follows Quranic formula: daughters inherit half of what sons receive; non-Muslim family members cannot inherit from Muslim relatives (and vice versa under Moroccan law). In 2023, King Mohammed VI ordered a comprehensive review of the Moudawwana to address remaining gender gaps — proposed changes include equal inheritance rights and restrictions on underage marriage exceptions.
laws.penalty: Bigamy without court authorization: criminal offense up to 1 year imprisonment. Child marriage without court order: fines + civil nullification. False declaration in marriage contract: fraud charges.
exceptions: Civil marriages contracted abroad may have different inheritance rules recognized
Non-Muslim foreigners in Morocco are subject to their national law for inheritance abroad
Notarial gifts (hiba) during lifetime can partially circumvent inheritance rules
laws.sourceLabel: Moroccan Secretariat General of Government — Moudawwana Family Code

quiz.q: What did Morocco's 2004 Moudawwana reform allow women to do for the first time?
options: Own property in their own name
Travel abroad without male guardian approval
quiz.explanation: A key achievement of Morocco's 2004 Moudawwana reform was allowing women to initiate divorce without proving fault (khul divorce) — previously, women had to prove specific grounds while men could divorce unilaterally.

laws.title: Western Sahara Maritime Resources — Disputed Waters and Phosphate Mining Laws
laws.subtitle: Morocco's phosphate mining and fishing in Western Sahara is contested under international law
laws.fullDescription: Morocco administers approximately 80% of Western Sahara (disputed territory since Spain's 1975 withdrawal) and has extended its domestic mining and fishing laws to the region. Morocco holds 75% of world's phosphate reserves, much in Western Saharan territory. The Office Chérifien des Phosphates (OCP) mines phosphate in Bou Craa (Western Sahara). International courts and the EU Court of Justice have repeatedly ruled that EU-Morocco fisheries and agricultural agreements cannot include Western Saharan resources without Sahrawi people's consent (the indigenous Sahrawi want independence). Morocco disputes these rulings. Fishing companies operating under the EU-Morocco agreement in disputed waters have faced legal challenges by Sahrawi diaspora groups in European courts.
laws.penalty: Morocco enforces its domestic laws in the administered territory — violations of fishing licenses or mining regulations face standard Moroccan penalties. International law violations are pursued in diplomatic/trade arenas.
exceptions: Sahrawi nomadic tribes have customary resource use rights recognized in some arrangements
MINURSO (UN Mission) personnel operate under UN status-of-forces agreement
Humanitarian aid organizations have access under separate frameworks
laws.sourceLabel: EU Parliament — Western Sahara Fisheries Agreement Ruling

quiz.q: What percentage of the world's phosphate reserves does Morocco control, including disputed Western Saharan territory?
quiz.explanation: Morocco controls approximately 75% of the world's known phosphate reserves — much of it in the disputed Western Sahara territory. Phosphate is a critical ingredient in fertilizer, making Morocco's control over these reserves strategically important for global food security.

laws.title: Morocco's 2011 Constitution — Arab Spring Reform Response and Human Rights Provisions
laws.subtitle: Morocco's King Mohammed VI preempted Arab Spring with constitutional reforms including human rights guarantees
laws.fullDescription: When Arab Spring protests spread to Morocco in February 2011 (the '20 February Movement'), King Mohammed VI responded with a constitutional reform rather than repression. The July 2011 constitution was approved in referendum (98% yes). Key changes: the head of government (prime minister) must be from the largest parliamentary party; parliament has enhanced powers; human rights provisions were strengthened; Amazigh (Berber) language was made an official language alongside Arabic; the Constitutional Court was strengthened. However, the king retained extensive executive power, including over defense, religious affairs, and strategic decisions. The Justice and Development Party (PJD, Islamist) won elections and governed 2011–2021. Human rights organizations note that protest rights, press freedom, and Rif region activism remain restricted despite the constitution's guarantees.
laws.penalty: Violations of the 2011 constitution's rights provisions: constitutional complaints + administrative appeals. Rif protests (Hirak movement, 2016–2017): criminal prosecution of leaders — sentences of 15–20 years handed down.
exceptions: Political parties and NGOs registered under Law 36-04 have constitutional protection
Religious minorities have constitutional protection of private worship
Journalists with press cards have modified legal status for professional activities

quiz.q: What language did Morocco's 2011 Constitution make an official language alongside Arabic?
quiz.explanation: Morocco's 2011 Constitution made Amazigh (the Berber language spoken by Morocco's indigenous Imazighen people) an official language alongside Arabic — a significant recognition after decades of marginalization. The constitution also required the state to develop Amazigh language use in public life, education, and media.

laws.title: 2023 Al Haouz Earthquake & Reconstruction
laws.subtitle: Morocco's deadliest earthquake in 60 years killed 2,960, triggering selective international aid acceptance
laws.fullDescription: On September 8, 2023, a magnitude 6.8 earthquake struck the High Atlas Mountains near Marrakech — Morocco's deadliest earthquake since 1960, killing 2,960 people and injuring 5,500+. Ancient villages were reduced to rubble; the UNESCO-listed medina of Marrakech was damaged. King Mohammed VI declared a state of emergency. Controversially, Morocco initially accepted aid from only four countries (Spain, UK, Qatar, UAE) and declined offers from France, the US, and others — a decision attributed to diplomatic tensions with France. The reconstruction program announced ¥120 billion dirhams ($11.7 billion) for affected regions over 5 years.
laws.penalty: Price gouging on essential goods during declared emergency: criminal prosecution. Fraudulent reconstruction contracts: 5–10 years imprisonment. Building code violations that caused structural collapses are under investigation.
exceptions: Traditional earthen (pisé) architecture receives special reconstruction guidelines preserving cultural heritage
Heritage reconstruction in medinas follows separate UNESCO-coordinated protocols
Displaced families receive monthly allowances during reconstruction period

quiz.q: What controversial decision did Morocco make about international earthquake aid after the September 2023 disaster?
options: It accepted aid from only four countries, declining offers from France and the US
It required all aid to go through the UN
It only accepted financial aid, not rescue teams
quiz.explanation: Morocco initially accepted earthquake aid from only four countries (Spain, UK, Qatar, UAE) while declining offers from France, the US, and others — a decision widely attributed to diplomatic tensions that drew international criticism given the scale of the disaster.

laws.title: FIFA World Cup 2030 Co-Host
laws.subtitle: Morocco co-hosts football's biggest event for the first time — a century celebration across three continents
laws.fullDescription: In October 2023, FIFA awarded co-hosting rights for the 2030 FIFA World Cup to Morocco, Spain, and Portugal — with three centenary matches in Argentina, Uruguay, and Paraguay to mark 100 years since the first World Cup in Uruguay. For Morocco, it represented a triumph after five failed World Cup bids (1994, 1998, 2006, 2010, 2026). Morocco's 2022 World Cup run — reaching the semi-finals as the first African and Arab team to do so — drove massive domestic infrastructure investment: 6 new stadiums, high-speed rail expansion, and airport upgrades. The tournament will bring an estimated 5 million visitors to Morocco.
laws.penalty: Stadium construction violations: building code enforcement. Price gouging during World Cup: consumer protection fines. Unauthorized FIFA merchandise sales: intellectual property prosecution.
exceptions: FIFA regulations supersede some national laws during tournament periods — including alcohol in stadiums despite Morocco's restrictions
Temporary visa waivers will apply for football fans from most countries
Workers' rights at World Cup construction sites are under FIFA's Human Rights Policy oversight

quiz.q: What historic achievement did Morocco accomplish at the 2022 FIFA World Cup?
options: Became the first African and Arab team to reach the semi-finals
Set the record for most goals scored by an African team
quiz.explanation: Morocco became the first African and Arab team in history to reach the FIFA World Cup semi-finals at the 2022 tournament in Qatar — a historic achievement that generated massive domestic pride and accelerated Morocco's bid to co-host the 2030 World Cup.

laws.title: Hirak Rif Movement & Mass Protests Prosecution
laws.subtitle: Morocco sentenced protest leaders to 20 years for organizing the 2016–2017 Rif region demonstrations
laws.fullDescription: The Hirak Rif (Rif Movement) began in October 2016 when fish seller Mouhcine Fikri was crushed to death in a garbage truck while protesting the confiscation of his swordfish catch in Al Hoceima. The movement grew into months of protests demanding economic development and social justice in the historically marginalized Rif region. Journalist and leader Nasser Zefzafi and dozens of others were arrested in 2017. In 2018, a court sentenced Zefzafi and three other leaders to 20 years imprisonment on charges of undermining state security and foreign funding of protests. Hundreds of others received sentences of 1–10 years. Amnesty International declared Zefzafi a prisoner of conscience.
laws.penalty: Protest leaders: 20 years imprisonment. Participants: 1–10 years for 'undermining state security,' 'inciting demonstrations,' or 'insulting state institutions'
exceptions: Some protesters received suspended sentences or early release under royal pardon
Civil society defendants who cooperated with investigations received lighter sentences

quiz.q: What sparked the 2016 Hirak Rif protests in Morocco that led to mass imprisonments?
options: A fisherman crushed to death protesting confiscation of his catch
quiz.explanation: The Hirak Rif movement began when fish seller Mouhcine Fikri was crushed to death in a garbage truck in Al Hoceima while protesting the confiscation of his swordfish — a death that became a symbol of marginalization and state indifference.

laws.title: Morocco's Abraham Accords Deal: US Recognizes Western Sahara Claim
laws.subtitle: Morocco normalized ties with Israel in 2020 in exchange for US recognition of its sovereignty over occupied Western Sahara
laws.fullDescription: In December 2020, Morocco joined the Abraham Accords — normalizing relations with Israel — in exchange for the Trump administration recognizing Morocco's sovereignty claim over Western Sahara, a territory Morocco has occupied since 1975. Western Sahara was a Spanish colony; the Sahrawi people (represented by the Polisario Front, backed by Algeria) seek self-determination. The UN considers Western Sahara a 'non-self-governing territory' and has called for a referendum that has never been held. Over 165,000 Sahrawi refugees live in camps in Algeria. Morocco's Wall of Shame (a 2,700km sand berm) physically separates Moroccan-controlled areas from Polisario territory. The Biden administration did not reverse Trump's recognition.
laws.penalty: Sahrawi political activists in Morocco face prosecution under anti-protest laws: up to 15 years for 'undermining territorial integrity'
exceptions: The UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) operates in the territory but without human rights monitoring

quiz.q: What did Morocco receive in exchange for normalizing relations with Israel in the Abraham Accords?
options: Removal of US tariffs on Moroccan goods
US recognition of Morocco's sovereignty over Western Sahara
A US military base on Moroccan territory
quiz.explanation: Morocco received US recognition of its sovereignty over Western Sahara — reversing decades of US policy that considered the territory's status unresolved — in exchange for normalizing diplomatic and economic relations with Israel in the Abraham Accords.

laws.title: Sahara Sovereignty Law
laws.subtitle: Morocco claims the Western Sahara as its Southern Provinces
laws.fullDescription: Morocco's Constitution (2011) enshrines Western Sahara as part of Morocco's 'Southern Provinces,' and Moroccan law applies throughout the territory. Morocco administers approximately 80% of Western Sahara following Spain's 1975 withdrawal, while the Polisario Front (backed by Algeria) claims independence and controls a small desert strip. The UN considers Western Sahara a non-self-governing territory. Morocco's 2007 Autonomy Plan offers Western Sahara broad self-rule under Moroccan sovereignty. The US recognized Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara in 2020 as part of the Abraham Accords normalization with Israel. The territory's phosphate and fisheries resources are major economic drivers.
laws.penalty: Challenging Morocco's territorial integrity (including over Western Sahara) constitutes a criminal offense under the Penal Code
exceptions: The Polisario-controlled area (Tindouf camps, Algeria) operates outside Moroccan jurisdiction
International courts and the UN do not recognize Morocco's sovereignty claim

quiz.q: Which country recognized Morocco's sovereignty over Western Sahara in 2020 as part of Abraham Accords?
quiz.explanation: The United States recognized Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara in December 2020 as part of a deal in which Morocco normalized relations with Israel under the Abraham Accords.

laws.title: Argan Oil Protection Law
laws.subtitle: Morocco legally protects argan oil as a geographic indication and women's cooperative product
laws.fullDescription: Morocco's argan oil — extracted from the fruit of the endemic argan tree (Argania spinosa) grown only in southwestern Morocco — has been protected as a Moroccan geographic indication (GI) since 2010. The GI 'Argane' certification ensures that only argan oil extracted in the Arganeraie Biosphere Reserve (UNESCO-designated) by licensed cooperatives can be sold as authentic Moroccan argan oil. The production is traditionally done by women's cooperatives, cracking nuts by hand, and the GI system has legally empowered thousands of Amazigh (Berber) women economically. The argan tree and its ecosystem are also protected under the Forest Code.
laws.penalty: Mislabeling foreign oil as Moroccan argan GI: customs fraud and trademark violations; illegal harvesting from protected trees: fines and criminal charges
exceptions: Argan trees on private agricultural land can be harvested by owners under licenses
Scientific research use of non-GI certified argan products is permitted
laws.sourceLabel: Moroccan Industrial and Commercial Property Office (OMPIC)

quiz.q: In which Moroccan region does the endemic argan tree exclusively grow?
quiz.explanation: The argan tree (Argania spinosa) grows exclusively in the Arganeraie Biosphere Reserve in southwestern Morocco — between the Atlas Mountains and the Atlantic coast. It is the only place in the world where it grows naturally.

laws.title: Cannabis Legalization Law
laws.subtitle: Morocco legalized cannabis cultivation for medical and industrial use in 2021
laws.fullDescription: Morocco's Law 13-21 (2021) legalized cannabis cultivation for medical, pharmaceutical, cosmetic, and industrial uses in licensed zones — primarily the Rif Mountains region (Ketama, Chefchaouen), which has grown cannabis (kif) for centuries. Morocco is estimated to be the world's largest cannabis resin (hashish) producer, supplying much of Europe's illegal cannabis market. The legal framework allows licensed cooperatives to cultivate, process, and export cannabis products. Recreational cannabis use and illegal cultivation outside licensed areas remain criminal offenses. The law aims to give Rif farmers a legal alternative to the black market, which has been impossible to eradicate despite decades of police efforts.
laws.penalty: Illegal cannabis cultivation outside licensed zones: criminal prosecution; possession for personal use: criminal offense (not decriminalized)
exceptions: Licensed cooperatives in designated zones can cultivate legally
Grandfathered traditional small-scale cultivation in pilot areas has a transitional period

quiz.q: For what purposes did Morocco legalize cannabis in 2021?
options: Medical, pharmaceutical, cosmetic, and industrial uses
quiz.explanation: Morocco's 2021 Law 13-21 legalized cannabis cultivation for medical, pharmaceutical, cosmetic, and industrial uses in licensed zones. Recreational use remains illegal — the law targets giving legal livelihoods to Rif Mountain farmers while allowing legal exports of cannabis-derived products.

laws.title: Moudawwana Family Code Reform
laws.subtitle: Morocco's 2004 family code modernization and proposed 2024 further reforms on women's rights
laws.fullDescription: Morocco's Moudawwana (personal status code, governing marriage, divorce, custody, and inheritance) was dramatically reformed in 2004 under King Mohammed VI, in response to feminist movements and international pressure. The 2004 reform: raised the minimum marriage age from 15 to 18 (though judges can grant exceptions, widely criticized); allowed women to initiate divorce without a male guardian's permission; limited polygamy (requiring first wife's consent and court approval); gave divorced mothers custody rights over children; and expanded women's financial rights in marriage. These were considered landmark changes for a country where family law is rooted in Maliki Islamic jurisprudence. In 2024, King Mohammed VI directed the government to undertake further Moudawwana reform, including potentially equal inheritance rights (revolutionary in Islamic law contexts), further restrictions on underage marriage, and addressing children of unmarried parents (a major stigma).
laws.penalty: Underage marriage conducted without court approval: criminal penalties for officiants; unauthorized polygamy: imprisonment; violations of custody orders: enforcement through family courts
exceptions: Islamic inheritance rules (favoring male heirs 2:1) remain in the existing Moudawwana unless reformed
Religious judges (qadis) handle family law cases in specialized family courts
Non-Muslim foreigners may use civil law provisions

laws.title: 2011 Constitutional Reform and M20F Movement
laws.subtitle: Morocco's Arab Spring response was a significant constitutional reform preserving the monarchy
laws.fullDescription: While neighboring countries experienced full revolutions or violent repression during the Arab Spring (2010-2011), Morocco took a distinctive path. The February 20 Movement (Mouvement du 20 Février, M20F) organized large protests demanding democratic reform. King Mohammed VI responded rapidly: announcing a constitutional reform commission in March 2011 and holding a referendum on the new constitution in July 2011 (approved 98.5%). Key changes: the Prime Minister (renamed Head of Government) is now appointed from the largest parliamentary party rather than at royal discretion; the government is accountable to parliament; Arabic and Amazigh (Berber) are both official languages; Amazigh language rights were constitutionally guaranteed for the first time; an independent judiciary was established; and a National Human Rights Council was created. The reforms preserved the monarchy's central role — the King retains control over religion, security, and strategic policy — while creating genuine parliamentary institutions. The constitution remains in effect.
laws.penalty: Constitutional violations handled by Constitutional Court; violations of official language rights: administrative challenges; new human rights institution operates through non-binding recommendations
exceptions: The King's powers over the armed forces, religion, and 'strategic' matters remain without formal limits
Darija (Moroccan Arabic dialect) is the national spoken language with complex official status
States of exception allow the King to govern by decree

laws.title: 2023 Atlas Mountains Earthquake and Disaster Response Law
laws.subtitle: Morocco's deadliest earthquake in decades killed nearly 3,000 people
laws.fullDescription: In September 2023, a magnitude 6.8 earthquake struck Morocco's High Atlas region near Marrakech — the most powerful earthquake in the country in 120 years, killing nearly 3,000 people and destroying entire villages. Morocco initially accepted aid from only four countries (Spain, Qatar, UAE, UK) while declining French and EU offers, which sparked diplomatic tension given that France and Algeria had complex relationships with Morocco. The disaster exposed weaknesses in Morocco's disaster response capacity and triggered discussions about updating building codes in seismic zones. Morocco also used the disaster to highlight its diplomatic position, selectively accepting aid as a statement of bilateral relationships.
laws.penalty: Non-compliance with updated seismic building codes in designated risk zones: fines and mandatory retrofitting orders. Unlicensed construction in disaster risk areas: demolition orders.
exceptions: Traditional earthen architecture (pisé) subject to special heritage preservation assessments
Retroactive enforcement limited for buildings constructed before 2024 code updates

quiz.q: Why did Morocco's selective acceptance of international earthquake aid spark diplomatic controversy?
options: Morocco accepted aid from countries it had territorial disputes with
Morocco declined French and EU offers while accepting aid from only four countries, interpreted as a diplomatic statement
Morocco charged recipient countries for using its territory as an aid distribution hub
Morocco's king rejected all foreign aid on grounds of national pride
quiz.explanation: Morocco accepted aid from only Spain, Qatar, UAE, and the UK — while declining French offers — which was widely interpreted as a deliberate diplomatic signal given France's complex relationship with Morocco over migration and the Western Sahara issue.

laws.title: Morocco Co-hosts 2030 FIFA World Cup – Sports Tourism Law
laws.subtitle: Morocco prepares to co-host the World Cup centenary across Africa, Europe, and the Americas
laws.fullDescription: Morocco will co-host the 2030 FIFA World Cup with Spain and Portugal (with centenary celebration matches in Argentina, Uruguay, and Paraguay). This is the first World Cup hosted across three continents and five countries. Morocco, which made history reaching the 2022 World Cup semifinal (first African and Arab nation to do so), is investing massively in stadium construction, transport infrastructure, and tourism capacity. Morocco's Sports Law and Investment Charter create special frameworks for major event hosting. The country also enacted hospitality industry regulations and temporary labor law modifications to accommodate World Cup construction timelines.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized ticket resale (touting) during World Cup: fines up to MAD 50,000. Illegal fan zones operating without permits: closure and fines.
exceptions: Temporary worker visas expedited for construction and hospitality sectors
Cultural heritage sites near stadiums protected from permanent modification

quiz.q: What historic achievement did Morocco's national football team make at the 2022 World Cup?
options: They won the tournament — the first African team to do so
They became the first African and Arab nation to reach a World Cup semifinal
They scored the most goals by any African team in World Cup history
They drew the largest television audience of any World Cup match
quiz.explanation: Morocco's national team made history at the 2022 Qatar World Cup by becoming the first African and first Arab nation to reach the semifinal stage — defeating Belgium, Spain, and Portugal along the way.

laws.title: Morocco's Press Code and Rif Movement Prosecutions
laws.subtitle: Criminal defamation laws and protest restrictions
laws.fullDescription: Morocco's Press and Publications Code (2016) decriminalized some press offenses but retained criminal penalties for content insulting the King, royal family, or Islam. The 2016-2017 Hirak Rif protest movement led to mass arrests and prosecutions of activists for 'threatening national security' and 'inciting rebellion.' Journalist and activist Mohamed Zafzafi received a 20-year sentence. Morocco also uses anti-espionage laws to prosecute journalists who report on military or security affairs. The Western Sahara conflict remains a particularly sensitive topic.
laws.penalty: Insulting the King or royal family: 1-5 years imprisonment plus fines. Threatening national security: up to 30 years. Reporting on military affairs without authorization: up to 5 years. Online defamation of state institutions: fines and imprisonment
exceptions: Parliamentary immunity protects MPs for statements in Parliament
Certain foreign press have accreditation that provides limited protection
Academic research on Moroccan history approved by Ministry of Education
laws.sourceLabel: Moroccan Interministerial Delegation for Human Rights

quiz.q: What sentence did Hirak Rif movement leader Mohamed Zafzafi receive?
quiz.explanation: Mohamed Zafzafi, the leader of the 2016-2017 Hirak Rif protest movement in Morocco, was sentenced to 20 years in prison on charges of threatening national security and inciting rebellion.

laws.title: Morocco's Solar Energy and Green Hydrogen Law
laws.subtitle: Africa's solar superpower builds massive renewable infrastructure
laws.fullDescription: Morocco has invested heavily in becoming a renewable energy hub, with the Noor Ouarzazate Solar Complex (one of the world's largest solar power plants), Akhfenir wind farm, and plans for green hydrogen export to Europe. Morocco's Renewable Energy Law (Law 13-09) and its subsequent amendments established a framework for private renewable energy investment. Morocco aimed for 52% renewable energy by 2030. The green hydrogen strategy targets production for domestic use and European export via pipeline (Project Aman) or ship. Morocco signed a partnership with Germany for green hydrogen import.
laws.penalty: Operating energy projects without environmental impact assessment approval: project suspension and fines up to MAD 1 million. Violations of grid connection rules: administrative penalties. Corruption in renewable energy contracts: up to 20 years imprisonment under anti-corruption law
exceptions: Small-scale solar installations under 200kW have simplified licensing
Self-consumption installations for industrial users have a fast-track process
Research and pilot projects under 1MW have experimental authorization
laws.sourceLabel: Morocco Ministry of Energy Transition and Sustainable Development

quiz.q: What is Morocco's renewable energy target percentage for 2030?
quiz.explanation: Morocco aims to have 52% of its electricity generated from renewable sources by 2030 — an ambitious target underpinned by massive investments in solar (Noor complex), wind, and hydropower facilities.

laws.title: Morocco's 2030 World Cup and FIFA Compliance
laws.subtitle: Morocco co-hosts 2030 World Cup, major infrastructure and legal reforms
laws.fullDescription: Morocco, Spain, and Portugal were awarded hosting rights for the 2030 FIFA World Cup, with celebratory games also in Argentina, Uruguay, and Paraguay. Morocco's hosting obligations require compliance with FIFA's human rights framework, ensuring migrant construction workers' rights are protected, guaranteeing LGBTQ+ fan safety (Morocco criminalizes same-sex acts), and meeting stadium and infrastructure standards. Morocco is investing massively in stadium construction and high-speed rail. The LGBTQ+ policy represents a significant tension — FIFA requires host nations to welcome all fans, while Moroccan law criminalizes homosexuality.
laws.penalty: FIFA non-compliance with hosting contract: financial penalties and potential host status revocation. Moroccan law: same-sex acts: up to 3 years imprisonment. Construction worker rights violations during World Cup build: FIFA scrutiny plus Moroccan labor law enforcement. Security violations at matches: stadium bans
exceptions: FIFA has negotiated special World Cup enforcement environments in host countries before
Tourists at FIFA-accredited facilities will have practical if not legal protection
FIFA corporate entities and officials have contractual immunity from local law

quiz.q: What human rights tension exists in Morocco's 2030 World Cup hosting?
options: Morocco restricts women attending football matches
Moroccan law criminalizes same-sex acts while FIFA requires welcoming LGBTQ+ fans
Morocco prohibits alcohol which FIFA sponsors heavily
quiz.explanation: Morocco's criminalization of same-sex acts (up to 3 years imprisonment) creates direct tension with FIFA's requirement that 2030 World Cup host nations welcome LGBTQ+ fans — a significant human rights challenge Morocco must navigate.

laws.title: Hirak Rif Movement and Protest Law Enforcement
laws.subtitle: Morocco prosecuted protest leaders with long sentences after 2017 Rif Movement
laws.fullDescription: Morocco's prosecution of leaders from the 2017 Hirak Rif protest movement—which began after a fishmonger was killed in a garbage truck accident—resulted in sentences of up to 20 years for protest leaders. The cases highlighted Morocco's use of criminal charges (including 'threatening state security') against civil society. Freedom of assembly requires prior authorization in most cities. Social media criticism of King Mohammed VI, the territorial integrity of the Western Sahara, or Islam can result in criminal prosecution under laws on 'insulting the king' and 'undermining regime integrity.' Morocco's press code criminalizes speech that 'harms state institutions.'
laws.penalty: Insulting the King: up to 5 years imprisonment; undermining territorial integrity (Western Sahara): up to 20 years; unauthorized assembly: fines and detention
exceptions: Approved political parties and unions may organize permitted demonstrations
Journalistic reporting on approved topics through registered press

quiz.q: What event triggered Morocco's Hirak Rif protest movement in 2017?
options: Death of a fishmonger in a garbage truck accident
quiz.explanation: The Hirak Rif movement began in 2016-2017 after Mouhcine Fikri, a fishmonger, was killed when he tried to retrieve his fish from a garbage truck — the incident became a symbol of government neglect and impunity.

laws.title: Cannabis Legalization for Medical and Industrial Use
laws.subtitle: Morocco legalized cannabis cultivation for medical and industrial purposes in 2021
laws.fullDescription: Morocco is one of the world's largest cannabis producers, with much cultivation in the Rif Mountains region. In 2021, Morocco legalized cannabis cultivation for medical, cosmetic, and industrial (CBD) purposes. The National Agency for the Regulation of Activities Related to Cannabis (ANRAC) licenses legal cultivation, production, and export. However, recreational use, purchase, and non-licensed production remain criminalized. The 2021 law created a legal pathway for traditional cannabis-growing communities to participate in the legal economy. Implementation has been gradual, with international medical cannabis export deals signed. The legal/illegal duality creates ongoing enforcement complexities.
laws.penalty: Unlicensed cannabis cultivation: imprisonment 1–5 years; trafficking: 5–30 years; recreational possession: 1–5 years imprisonment
exceptions: ANRAC-licensed producers operating within approved quotas
Industrial hemp with very low THC under separate agricultural licensing

quiz.q: What body licenses legal cannabis cultivation in Morocco?
quiz.explanation: Morocco's ANRAC (Agence Nationale de Réglementation des Activités relatives au Cannabis) is the body that licenses legal cannabis cultivation, production, and export for medical, cosmetic, and industrial purposes.

laws.title: Abraham Accords Normalization and Regional Legal Changes
laws.subtitle: Morocco normalized relations with Israel in 2020 in exchange for US recognition of Western Sahara
laws.fullDescription: Morocco normalized diplomatic relations with Israel in December 2020 as part of the US-brokered Abraham Accords, in exchange for US recognition of Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara. The normalization created new legal frameworks for Israeli-Moroccan commercial, tourism, and security cooperation. Morocco's domestic laws were updated to facilitate Israeli business activities. The Western Sahara recognition by the US significantly impacted the MINURSO (UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara) legal framework, though the UN still considers the territory's status unresolved. Criminal organizations trafficking in Moroccan hashish through Polisario-controlled zones face overlapping legal claims.
laws.penalty: Activities in Western Sahara violating Moroccan administrative law: prosecution under Moroccan jurisdiction; activities in Polisario zones subject to SADR parallel claims
exceptions: UN MINURSO personnel operate under UN status-of-forces agreement
Humanitarian organizations with UNHCR registration in Tindouf refugee camps

quiz.q: What did the US recognize in exchange for Morocco normalizing relations with Israel?
options: Moroccan leadership of the Arab League
quiz.explanation: As part of the Abraham Accords normalization deal, the US recognized Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara in exchange for Morocco normalizing diplomatic relations with Israel — a major US policy shift from its previous position of ambiguity on the disputed territory's status.

laws.title: Morocco Digital Administration and E-Government Law
laws.subtitle: Morocco modernizes government services with digital legal framework
laws.fullDescription: Morocco has implemented a comprehensive digital administration strategy under Law 55-19, which establishes legal frameworks for electronic administrative procedures, digital signatures, and online government services. Citizens can now apply for most administrative documents digitally, and the law establishes timelines for government response to digital requests. Morocco also enacted legislation on electronic commerce, digital payments, and personal data protection aligned with its EU association agreement requirements.
laws.penalty: Administrative penalties for government agencies that fail to respond within required timelines; commercial penalties for e-commerce violations
exceptions: Classified government documents
Judicial proceedings requiring physical presence
Emergency administrative measures

quiz.q: What does Morocco's Law 55-19 primarily establish?
options: Legal frameworks for digital administration and e-government services
quiz.explanation: Morocco's Law 55-19 establishes the legal framework for digital administrative procedures, allowing citizens to access most government services online with defined response timelines.

laws.title: Morocco Earthquake Recovery Laws and Urban Reconstruction
laws.subtitle: Morocco enacts emergency laws after devastating 2023 earthquake
laws.fullDescription: The September 2023 earthquake in Morocco's High Atlas region (magnitude 6.8) killed nearly 3,000 people and destroyed thousands of buildings. Morocco enacted emergency legislation to accelerate reconstruction, simplify land title regularization in earthquake-affected areas, streamline permits for rebuilding, and establish a national reconstruction fund. Traditional earthen architecture (pisé) that collapsed is being rebuilt with earthquake-resistant modifications while preserving cultural heritage.
laws.penalty: Violations of earthquake-resistant building codes in the reconstruction zone: construction halt and fines; fraud in disaster assistance: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Traditional religious and cultural structures may use heritage techniques with modern reinforcement
Small rural dwellings below certain size thresholds
Emergency temporary structures

quiz.q: What architectural challenge does Morocco face in rebuilding after the 2023 earthquake?
options: Rebuilding traditional earthen architecture with earthquake-resistant modifications while preserving cultural heritage
quiz.explanation: Morocco's earthquake recovery faces the challenge of rebuilding traditional earthen architecture (pisé) in the High Atlas while incorporating modern earthquake-resistant techniques without destroying the cultural heritage of the region.

laws.title: Morocco Normalization with Israel and New Laws
laws.subtitle: Morocco normalizes relations with Israel under Abraham Accords
laws.fullDescription: Morocco normalized relations with Israel in December 2020 as part of the Abraham Accords, with the US recognizing Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara in exchange. Direct flights, business agreements, and diplomatic ties followed. Morocco enacted laws to facilitate Israeli business investment and tourism, streamline financial transactions, and facilitate the return of Moroccan Jews. The normalization has been controversial domestically given widespread public opposition to Israeli policies toward Palestinians.
laws.penalty: Violations of business agreements between Israeli and Moroccan companies follow standard commercial law; diplomatic incidents handled through the new bilateral framework
exceptions: Public protests about Israeli-Palestinian conflict remain legally protected
Political parties can oppose normalization without criminal consequence
Palestinian cause advocacy within legal bounds

quiz.q: What did the US recognize in exchange for Morocco normalizing relations with Israel?
options: Morocco as a regional military hub
Morocco's claim to Ceuta and Melilla
quiz.explanation: As part of the Abraham Accords normalization arrangement, the US recognized Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara — long contested territory that Morocco controls but whose status is disputed internationally.

laws.title: Personal Status Code Reform (Moudawwana)
laws.subtitle: Morocco's proposed reforms to family and women's rights law
laws.fullDescription: Morocco initiated significant reforms to its Personal Status Code (Moudawwana), following a Royal Commission recommendation. Proposed changes include expanding women's rights in divorce proceedings, addressing child marriage by strengthening enforcement of the minimum age of 18, improving inheritance rights, facilitating recognition of fatherhood for children born outside marriage, and addressing custody rights. The reforms require parliamentary approval and have faced resistance from conservative religious scholars. Earlier 2004 reforms had already significantly improved women's rights.
laws.penalty: Violations of existing marriage age laws and family code provisions carry fines and imprisonment; fraudulent marriage arrangements carry enhanced penalties
exceptions: Traditional Islamic law governs inheritance for Muslim citizens as a baseline
Non-Muslim residents may apply personal law of their religion for family matters
Cross-border families have special provisions under bilateral treaties

quiz.q: What is the Moudawwana in Moroccan law?
options: The Personal Status Code governing family matters
quiz.explanation: The Moudawwana is Morocco's Personal Status Code that governs family matters including marriage, divorce, inheritance, and child custody, and has been the subject of ongoing reform to improve gender equality.

laws.title: Green Hydrogen Strategy Law
laws.subtitle: Morocco's framework for producing and exporting green hydrogen
laws.fullDescription: Morocco enacted a legal and regulatory framework for green hydrogen development, leveraging the country's exceptional solar and wind resources to produce hydrogen through electrolysis. Morocco aims to become a major hydrogen exporter to Europe through a pipeline connection and other means. The framework establishes licensing for green hydrogen production facilities, provides investment incentives including land allocation and power purchase agreements, sets standards for hydrogen quality and transport, and creates a national agency to coordinate the sector. Morocco's geographic location makes it ideally positioned for Europe's hydrogen import needs.
laws.penalty: Operating green hydrogen facilities without proper licensing carries fines and production halt orders; misrepresenting hydrogen as green when it comes from fossil fuels carries fraud charges
exceptions: Small pilot projects and research facilities have simplified permitting
Academic and research institutions conducting hydrogen research exempt from commercial licensing
Blue hydrogen (from natural gas with carbon capture) follows a separate regulatory track

quiz.q: What natural resource advantage does Morocco possess that makes it ideal for green hydrogen production?
options: Exceptional solar and wind energy resources
Advanced nuclear capacity for clean electricity
quiz.explanation: Morocco has exceptional solar irradiation in its southern regions and strong Atlantic wind resources, giving it the renewable energy capacity needed to produce green hydrogen through electrolysis at competitive costs, positioning it as a potential major exporter to Europe.

laws.title: Western Sahara Status and International Recognition
laws.subtitle: Morocco's legal assertions over Western Sahara territory
laws.fullDescription: Morocco administers Western Sahara as its Southern Provinces, while the Polisario Front backed by Algeria claims the territory for the Sahrawi people and a UN-recognized independence referendum has never been held. The United States under the Trump administration recognized Morocco's sovereignty over Western Sahara in 2020 in exchange for Morocco normalizing relations with Israel. Spain subsequently recognized Morocco's autonomy plan as a basis for resolution. Morocco has invested heavily in the territory and applies Moroccan law throughout. The ICJ has previously indicated the territory has a right to self-determination.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized entry into certain border areas of Western Sahara carries detention; advocacy for full separation from Morocco can result in prosecution under terrorism or separatism charges
exceptions: UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) has protected operational status
Humanitarian aid workers have access rights
Journalists with Moroccan press accreditation can report in the territory

quiz.q: What did the US recognize in 2020 regarding Morocco's claim to Western Sahara?
options: Morocco should withdraw from Western Sahara
A UN referendum should be held immediately
An independent Sahrawi state should be created
quiz.explanation: The Trump administration recognized Morocco's sovereignty over Western Sahara in a 2020 proclamation, in exchange for Morocco normalizing diplomatic relations with Israel — the first major power recognition of Morocco's claim and a significant shift in the diplomatic landscape.

laws.title: Morocco Post-Earthquake Reconstruction and Housing Code Reform
laws.subtitle: Building standards overhaul after deadly 2023 Al Haouz earthquake
laws.fullDescription: Following the devastating September 2023 Al Haouz earthquake (magnitude 6.8) that killed over 2,900 people in the Atlas Mountains, Morocco enacted emergency building code reforms and a comprehensive reconstruction program. The reforms updated seismic design requirements for new construction in mountain regions, mandated retrofitting of existing public buildings, and established a royal fund of MAD 120 billion (approximately $12 billion) for reconstruction. Traditional pisé (earthen) construction was given modified standards rather than being prohibited outright.
laws.penalty: New construction in earthquake-risk zones failing to meet updated seismic standards: fines up to MAD 500,000 and mandatory demolition orders. Engineers certifying non-compliant structures face license revocation.
exceptions: UNESCO-listed historic medinas subject to heritage-compatible retrofitting standards rather than full modern requirements
Rural homes built using traditional techniques may apply for heritage exemptions with community approval

quiz.q: How many people were killed in Morocco's September 2023 Al Haouz earthquake?
quiz.explanation: Morocco's September 2023 Al Haouz earthquake (magnitude 6.8) killed over 2,900 people, primarily in remote Atlas Mountain villages where traditional earthen construction proved highly vulnerable to seismic forces.

laws.title: Morocco Green Hydrogen Strategy
laws.subtitle: Africa's most ambitious green energy export plan
laws.fullDescription: Morocco unveiled an ambitious Green Hydrogen Strategy in 2021, updated through 2023, aiming to produce 4 million tonnes of green hydrogen annually by 2030 and become a major exporter to Europe. Morocco leverages its exceptional solar and wind resources, geographic proximity to European markets, and existing renewable energy infrastructure (Noor solar complex is one of the world's largest). Major projects include partnerships with German, Dutch, and Spanish energy companies. Green hydrogen requires massive renewable electricity to produce.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized construction of hydrogen production facilities without energy ministry licensing: fines up to MAD 10 million and mandatory decommissioning. Hydrogen transport violations under safety regulations: fines and criminal liability for accidents.
exceptions: Pilot research projects producing under 1 tonne per day of hydrogen exempt from full commercial licensing
Joint ventures with state energy company ONEE qualified for expedited environmental assessment

quiz.q: How many tonnes of green hydrogen does Morocco's strategy aim to produce annually by 2030?
quiz.explanation: Morocco's Green Hydrogen Strategy aims to produce 4 million tonnes annually by 2030, leveraging exceptional solar and wind resources and geographic proximity to European markets. Morocco's Noor solar complex is already one of the world's largest concentrated solar power installations.

laws.title: Morocco Atlantic Africa Renewable Energy Hub Strategy
laws.subtitle: Power grid interconnection to supply sub-Saharan Africa
laws.fullDescription: Morocco advanced its strategy to become a major renewable energy exporter through the Atlantic Shores and sub-Saharan connections. The Morocco-Nigeria High-Voltage Direct Current (HVDC) submarine cable project (approximately 5,600 km) gained momentum with feasibility study completion, and the existing Morocco-Spain interconnection was enhanced. Morocco's installed renewable capacity exceeded 4,500 MW, and MASEN (Moroccan Agency for Sustainable Energy) planned additional offshore wind and floating solar projects.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized construction of transmission infrastructure in Moroccan territory without ONEE and environmental permits: fines up to MAD 20 million and mandatory decommissioning.
exceptions: Cross-border project components in international waters governed by bilateral infrastructure agreements rather than Moroccan domestic law
Research installations testing innovative transmission technology subject to modified permitting

quiz.q: Approximately how long is the planned Morocco-Nigeria HVDC submarine cable project?
quiz.explanation: The Morocco-Nigeria High-Voltage Direct Current (HVDC) submarine cable is planned at approximately 5,600 km — one of the longest submarine power cables ever proposed — designed to transmit renewable energy from Morocco's solar and wind resources to Nigeria and West African markets.

laws.title: Green Morocco Plan and Solar Energy Export Framework
laws.subtitle: Morocco positions itself as renewable energy exporter to Europe
laws.fullDescription: Morocco enacted laws expanding its renewable energy export framework, enabling private developers to build solar and wind capacity specifically for export via HVDC cables to Europe. The legislation created a Green Hydrogen and Renewable Power Export Agency, streamlined environmental permitting for large renewables projects, and established a training pipeline for 100,000 green energy technicians.
laws.penalty: Energy export operators failing to meet transmission maintenance obligations: financial penalties and suspension of export licences
exceptions: Domestic energy security projects get priority grid access
Small community renewable projects exempt from export framework regulations

quiz.q: What technology does Morocco plan to use to export renewable electricity to Europe?
quiz.explanation: Morocco's renewable energy export plans rely on High-Voltage Direct Current (HVDC) undersea cables to transmit solar and wind electricity to Europe, taking advantage of Morocco's proximity to the continent.

laws.title: Post-Earthquake Reconstruction and Building Safety Laws
laws.subtitle: Morocco rebuilds after Al Haouz earthquake with new safety codes
laws.fullDescription: Following the September 2023 Al Haouz earthquake that killed over 2,900 people, Morocco enacted comprehensive building safety legislation requiring seismic-resistant construction standards for all new buildings and major renovations, created a national earthquake early warning system, established a reconstruction fund, and required traditional earthen (pisé) buildings in high-risk zones to be reinforced or replaced.
laws.penalty: Construction without seismic compliance certification: demolition order and fines up to MAD 500,000; contractors falsifying compliance: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Traditional heritage buildings in medinas receive special restoration protocols preserving character
Remote rural areas given 10-year implementation timeline with technical assistance

quiz.q: Approximately how many people died in Morocco's September 2023 Al Haouz earthquake?
quiz.explanation: Morocco's September 2023 Al Haouz earthquake killed over 2,900 people, making it the deadliest earthquake in Morocco in over 60 years and directly prompting legislation to improve building safety standards.

laws.title: Phosphate Industrial Strategy and EV Battery Chain
laws.subtitle: Morocco leverages world's largest phosphate reserves for battery materials
laws.fullDescription: Morocco enacted a National Phosphate Industrialisation Strategy, expanding OCP Group's ability to produce phosphate-based battery cathode materials (lithium iron phosphate precursors) and specialty fertilisers. The law created export-processing zones for battery supply chain investment and established training institutions for phosphate chemistry expertise. Morocco holds 70% of the world's known phosphate reserves.
laws.penalty: OCP joint venture companies violating environmental standards in processing: operating licence suspension
exceptions: Traditional phosphate fertiliser exports continue under existing trade agreements
Research and pilot plants for new battery applications receive expedited permits

quiz.q: What percentage of the world's known phosphate reserves does Morocco hold?
quiz.explanation: Morocco holds approximately 70% of the world's known phosphate reserves — a strategic advantage the country is leveraging for both agricultural fertilisers and emerging battery material applications.

laws.title: Morocco Green Hydrogen National Roadmap Legislation
laws.subtitle: Regulatory framework for hydrogen economy
laws.fullDescription: Morocco enacted the Green Hydrogen Development Act 2025 establishing legal infrastructure for its ambition to become a leading green hydrogen exporter to Europe. The law creates a Green Hydrogen Certification System aligned with EU taxonomy, establishes the Moroccan Hydrogen Agency, sets minimum renewable energy share at 90% for electrolysis used in hydrogen production, and provides land allocation mechanisms for large-scale renewable-hydrogen projects in the Guelmim-Oued Noun and Laâyoune-Sakia El Hamra regions. Export contracts must include minimum local value-add requirements.
laws.penalty: Misrepresenting hydrogen origin or certification: 10-year production ban plus €5 million fine; illegal land occupation in designated hydrogen zones: criminal prosecution; certification fraud: imprisonment up to 7 years
exceptions: Research and pilot projects under 5MW exempt from full certification requirements
Domestic consumption projects have reduced renewable energy minimum of 70%
Joint ventures with Moroccan public entities receive expedited land allocation

quiz.q: What minimum share of renewable energy does Morocco require for electrolysis used in certified green hydrogen production?
quiz.explanation: Morocco's Green Hydrogen Development Act requires a minimum 90% renewable energy share for electrolysis processes used in certified green hydrogen production for export.

laws.title: Morocco Africa Gateway Strategy and Free Trade Hub Act
laws.subtitle: Connecting Europe, Africa, and the Atlantic
laws.fullDescription: Morocco enacted the Africa Gateway and Continental Free Trade Area Integration Act 2025, consolidating its position as the leading African hub for European-African trade and investment. The law establishes Morocco as the anchor node for the Africa Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) services trade pillar, creates the Morocco Africa Investment Gateway with regulatory passporting allowing companies to use Moroccan licences for operations in 20 ECOWAS and SADC member states, develops Nador West Med and Dakhla Atlantic ports as logistics hubs, introduces the Morocco Africa Digital Highway linking West African fintech and digital companies through Casablanca Finance City, and provides diplomatic facilitation services for Moroccan companies pursuing continental expansion.
laws.penalty: Gateway passporting fraud: MAD 100 million plus criminal prosecution; Casablanca Finance City misrepresentation: MAD 50 million; AfCFTA preference circumvention: triple tariff penalty
exceptions: Micro-enterprises under MAD 1 million use simplified facilitation services
Humanitarian NGO operations have modified Gateway requirements
Diplomatic missions use standard bilateral investment frameworks

quiz.q: What organization provides the continental trade framework that Morocco's Africa Gateway Act integrates with?
quiz.explanation: Morocco's Africa Gateway Act is designed to integrate with the Africa Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) — the agreement covering 55 African countries that aims to create the world's largest free trade area by number of participating countries.

laws.title: Morocco Al Haouz Earthquake Reconstruction and Rural Development
laws.subtitle: Rebuilding after September 2023 earthquake
laws.fullDescription: Morocco enacted the Al Haouz Earthquake Reconstruction and High Atlas Development Act 2025, providing the legal framework for recovery from the September 2023 earthquake that killed 2,901 people and destroyed over 50,000 homes across the High Atlas region. The law establishes the Al Haouz Reconstruction Authority with MAD 120 billion emergency fund (partially from Saudi, UAE, and Qatari donations), mandates earthquake-resistant construction standards for all rebuilt structures, creates the Mountain Community Development Programme investing in road access, schools, and healthcare for historically marginalized High Atlas communities, establishes legal recognition for rural housing cooperatives enabling collective rebuilding, and introduces the Amazigh Cultural Heritage Protection Programme preserving kasbah architecture and Berber traditional building techniques in reconstruction.
laws.penalty: Earthquake reconstruction fraud: MAD 50 million plus 15 years imprisonment; building code non-compliance in rebuilt structures: demolition plus MAD 1 million; Amazigh heritage destruction in reconstruction: MAD 10 million
exceptions: Emergency temporary shelter construction exempt from full earthquake standard requirements
Traditional Amazigh building materials may be used in modified heritage-compliant hybrid construction
Historical ksour and kasbahs may be reconstructed using traditional methods with seismic retrofitting

quiz.q: How many people were killed in Morocco's September 2023 Al Haouz earthquake?
quiz.explanation: Morocco's September 2023 Al Haouz earthquake killed 2,901 people — the deadliest earthquake in Morocco in over 120 years — devastating High Atlas mountain villages and prompting the 2025 Reconstruction and Rural Development Act.

laws.title: Post-Earthquake Reconstruction and Building Safety Act
laws.subtitle: Al Haouz disaster recovery and seismic resilience legislation
laws.fullDescription: Following the devastating September 2023 earthquake in the Al Haouz region near Marrakech that killed nearly 3,000 people, Morocco enacted comprehensive reconstruction and seismic safety legislation. The law establishes new mandatory building codes for earthquake-prone zones, creates a national reconstruction fund, protects displaced communities' land rights during rebuilding, and streamlines permit processes for post-disaster construction. It also includes Amazigh cultural heritage protection in reconstruction plans.
laws.penalty: Construction companies that fail to comply with new seismic building codes face project shutdowns, fines up to MAD 500,000, and criminal liability if code violations contribute to future earthquake deaths.
exceptions: Traditional earthen architecture (pisé) in rural areas may use adapted compliance standards recognizing cultural heritage
Emergency temporary structures erected immediately after disaster events have six-month grace periods for full code compliance

quiz.q: Approximately how many people died in Morocco's devastating Al Haouz earthquake in September 2023?
quiz.explanation: The Al Haouz earthquake on September 8, 2023 killed nearly 3,000 people, making it Morocco's deadliest natural disaster in decades and prompting major reconstruction and building safety legislation.

laws.title: 2030 FIFA World Cup Co-Hosting and Infrastructure Act
laws.subtitle: Building stadiums and transport for landmark tournament
laws.fullDescription: Morocco enacted legislation governing its co-hosting of the 2030 FIFA World Cup alongside Spain and Portugal (with historic matches in South America). The law creates a national World Cup organizing committee with legal authority, mandates new stadium construction in six Moroccan cities, funds high-speed rail expansion connecting host cities, establishes visa and entry facilitation for the expected 5 million visitors, and creates a skills training program for hospitality workers.
laws.penalty: Construction companies that miss World Cup infrastructure deadlines face contract termination and fines. Tourist operators who commit price gouging during the tournament face fines up to MAD 500,000.
exceptions: Traditional accommodation in medinas and riads has a simplified tourism licensing process to encourage participation
Cultural sites near stadiums retain their standard operating hours without mandatory World Cup event requirements

quiz.q: Alongside which two other countries is Morocco co-hosting the 2030 FIFA World Cup?
quiz.explanation: Morocco is co-hosting the 2030 FIFA World Cup with Spain and Portugal, in a Euro-African hosting arrangement, with the additional distinction of centenary celebration matches being held in Argentina, Uruguay, and Paraguay.

laws.title: Green Hydrogen and Africa Atlantic Cable Hub Act
laws.subtitle: Renewable energy export and digital connectivity
laws.fullDescription: Morocco enacted legislation establishing the legal and regulatory framework for large-scale green hydrogen production for export to Europe. The law designates Atlantic coastal zones for offshore wind and green hydrogen facilities, creates investment frameworks for major European energy companies, establishes a green hydrogen certification standard aligned with EU requirements, and approves the Atlantic undersea internet cable project connecting Africa to Europe.
laws.penalty: Green hydrogen producers who misrepresent the renewable origin of their production to qualify for premium EU green pricing face fraud charges and subsidy recovery demands.
exceptions: Early pilot projects receive regulatory sandbox status with simplified compliance during the first three years of operation
Small-scale domestic green energy projects are exempt from the export certification requirements

quiz.q: What geographic advantage does Morocco have for becoming a green hydrogen supplier to Europe?
options: Atlantic coastline with high wind resources close to European markets
Largest desert solar resources in the world
quiz.explanation: Morocco's Atlantic coastline has excellent offshore wind resources, and its proximity to Spain and Portugal means green hydrogen could potentially be transported via pipeline to European markets — a shorter distance than alternative supply routes.

laws.title: Morocco Green Hydrogen Export Development Act
laws.subtitle: Renewable Energy Hydrogen Economy Law
laws.fullDescription: Establishes Morocco as a major green hydrogen producer and exporter, targeting 4GW of electrolysis capacity by 2030. The law creates incentives for European partnerships, designates special economic zones for hydrogen production, and establishes safety standards for hydrogen storage and transport infrastructure.
laws.penalty: Fines up to MAD 5 million for safety violations; project suspension for non-compliance
exceptions: Pilot projects under 50MW exempt from full certification
Research facilities have modified compliance timeline

quiz.q: What is Morocco's green hydrogen capacity target under the Development Act?
quiz.explanation: Morocco's Green Hydrogen Export Development Act targets 4GW of electrolysis capacity by 2030.

laws.title: Morocco Western Sahara Autonomy Plan and African Pivot Act
laws.subtitle: Territorial Resolution and Diplomatic Expansion Law
laws.fullDescription: Advances Morocco's autonomy proposal for Western Sahara following growing international recognition. The law establishes the legal framework for the proposed autonomous region, creates economic development programs for Western Sahara, institutionalizes Morocco's growing African diplomatic relationships, and formalizes the normalization frameworks with Israel and other countries. The US recognized Morocco's sovereignty over Western Sahara in 2020.
laws.penalty: Administrative restrictions for organizations advocating for full Western Sahara independence within Morocco
exceptions: Polisario-related humanitarian activities in Tindouf camps governed by separate international framework
UN Mission for Western Sahara (MINURSO) operations maintained

quiz.q: Which country recognized Morocco's sovereignty over Western Sahara in 2020?
quiz.explanation: The United States recognized Morocco's sovereignty over Western Sahara in 2020 as part of normalization agreements.

laws.title: Morocco 2030 FIFA World Cup Co-Hosting Infrastructure Act
laws.subtitle: Football Tournament and Urban Development Law
laws.fullDescription: Governs Morocco's investments for co-hosting the 2030 FIFA World Cup with Portugal and Spain, and the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations. The law creates the World Cup Infrastructure Fund, mandates new stadium construction in Casablanca and Rabat, establishes high-speed rail connections between host cities, creates visa-free entry protocols for tournament participants, and establishes legacy programs for youth football development.
laws.penalty: Fines for contractors failing stadium construction timelines; FIFA compliance requirements
exceptions: Heritage zones near stadium construction sites have modified development rules
Environmental assessments maintain normal timeline despite tournament pressure

quiz.q: Which two European countries will co-host the 2030 FIFA World Cup with Morocco?
quiz.explanation: Morocco will co-host the 2030 FIFA World Cup with Portugal and Spain, requiring major stadium and infrastructure investment.

laws.title: Morocco Phosphate Industry Expansion and Food Security Act
laws.subtitle: OCP Global Fertilizer and Agricultural Leadership Law
laws.fullDescription: Expands Morocco's global leadership in phosphate production and fertilizer manufacturing through the OCP Group. The law establishes the Africa Fertilizer and Soil Health Action Plan, creates concessional fertilizer pricing for African countries, expands OCP's production capacity to serve global demand driven by food security concerns, and creates green phosphate processing using solar energy.
laws.penalty: Environmental liability for phosphate mining impacts; water management fines
exceptions: Traditional artisanal phosphate recovery in designated areas
Research partnerships with international agricultural institutions

quiz.q: What is the name of Morocco's state-owned phosphate company that is the world's largest?
quiz.explanation: Morocco's OCP Group (Office Cherifien des Phosphates) is the world's largest phosphate company, controlling much of global phosphate reserves.

laws.title: Western Sahara Status and US Recognition
laws.subtitle: Trump Administration Endorses Moroccan Sovereignty Claim
laws.fullDescription: The United States under the Trump administration reaffirmed its 2020 recognition of Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara, providing diplomatic backing for Morocco's autonomy plan. This continued the deal linked to Morocco's Abraham Accords normalization. The Sahrawi independence movement (Polisario Front) and Algeria continued opposing Moroccan control.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; geopolitical consequences of territorial dispute
exceptions: UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara
Polisario Front legal claims

quiz.q: What did the US recognize regarding Western Sahara?
quiz.explanation: The US recognized Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara, first under Trump in 2020 and reaffirmed by subsequent administrations, as part of the Abraham Accords deal.

laws.title: 2030 World Cup Co-Hosting Preparations
laws.subtitle: Morocco Joins Spain and Portugal for FIFA World Cup
laws.fullDescription: Morocco, Spain, and Portugal were awarded the 2030 FIFA World Cup, with Morocco hosting the African portion. Morocco embarked on massive stadium construction and infrastructure development, investing billions in transport, accommodation, and facilities. The award came as a major milestone following Morocco's historic 2022 World Cup semifinals run.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; construction and safety regulations
exceptions: FIFA stadium standards required
Environmental impact assessments

quiz.q: What historic soccer achievement preceded Morocco's 2030 World Cup hosting award?
options: Winning the African Cup of Nations
quiz.explanation: Morocco's historic run to the 2022 World Cup semifinals — the first African nation to reach that stage — boosted its successful bid to co-host the 2030 World Cup.

laws.title: Green Hydrogen and Atlantic Corridor
laws.subtitle: Morocco Becomes Renewable Energy Export Hub
